titre: Ultramarine, the Blue That Cost More Than Gold
accroche: In an old master painting, the blue of the Virgin's cloak is not a theological choice: it is a line item, pricier than gold by weight.
contenu_vulgarise:
In Renaissance religious painting, the most intense blue in a picture is not just a compositional choice: it is also a line item of cost. This blue, ultramarine, is made from lapis lazuli, a semi-precious stone extracted almost exclusively from the mines of Afghanistan's Badakhshan province, the same deposits worked for millennia.

## The price of a color

Extracting a pure pigment from the raw stone, full of white calcite and golden pyrite, requires a long purification process: the ground lapis lazuli is kneaded into a paste of wax and resin, then washed several times, each wash yielding a slightly less pure grade of blue than the one before. The most concentrated result, reserved for the most prestigious uses, could, at certain times, cost more than gold by the same weight: a 2020 study by the Rijksmuseum, the University of Amsterdam, VU Amsterdam, and the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in Grenoble, published in the journal *Science Advances*, notes this in passing about the seventeenth century. The study's own contribution lies elsewhere: some period recipes prescribed heating the stone red-hot before grinding it, a step that improved the pigment's yield; by X-raying five paintings from the fifteenth and seventeenth centuries, held at the Louvre, the Rijksmuseum, and the Mauritshuis, the study found in each one the chemical signature specific to that heating, confirming that the old masters had indeed followed the prescription.

Beyond the painter's fee, patrons often had to buy the gold and lapis lazuli going into the painting themselves, rather than leave that cost to the painter. Painters then economized by reserving ultramarine for the most visible elements (the robe of the Virgin or the Child) and replacing it elsewhere, notably as an underlayer, with a cheaper blue, azurite.

## A blue that shows its price

This economics sheds light on a convention usually read as purely religious: why, in so many old paintings, does the Virgin Mary wear the most intensely blue cloak in the whole scene. Ultramarine is used above all to mark the most important figures in a composition, Mary and the Child foremost among them. Dressing the Virgin in the most expensive pigment available is therefore not just a theological choice: it is also a way, for the patron buying that pigment himself, to display both his wealth and his devotion in the same place, as legible to a Renaissance eye as a price tag.

repere.texte: By the seventeenth century, ultramarine could cost more than gold by equal weight. A 2020 X-ray study, on five paintings from the fifteenth and seventeenth centuries, confirmed that painters did follow an old prescription: heating the lapis lazuli stone red-hot before grinding it, to improve its yield.
repere.source: Rijksmuseum, University of Amsterdam, VU Amsterdam, and ESRF, Science Advances, 2020

carte.punch: The blue of the Virgin's cloak is often the priciest line in the painter's contract.
carte.idee: Made from Afghan lapis lazuli, ultramarine could cost more than gold by weight. Patrons often bought it themselves and reserved it for the most important figures, which is why the Virgin's cloak is so intensely blue.

quiz.question: Why is the blue of the Virgin Mary's cloak so often the most intense in old paintings?
choix: Because ultramarine could cost more than gold, and reserving it for the Virgin displayed the patron's wealth and piety
Because blue was the only color painters could make without risk of fading over time
Because a rule of the Church required this exact color for the Virgin, under penalty of sanction
Because painting workshops had an unlimited supply of this color, unlike other pigments
quiz.explication: Ultramarine, made from lapis lazuli, could cost more than gold by weight: reserving it for the Virgin displayed both her central place in the scene and the wealth, and therefore the piety, of the patron who often bought this pigment himself. Nothing suggests a Church rule or an unlimited supply.
